en: Have all been laid waste.
Our heroes who boasted of valor—
May our mighty backs be broken.
What are turmoil and strife?
If you wish, behold them here!”
So saying, Külchoro continued:
“I shall spill your blood like water.
I shall bring your life to a clean end,
Cutting off your head like this,
And offer up your young life.
Sarybai, son of the ogre,
Why are you so wildly enraged?
Why rage and stir up strife,
When we have not carried off your land,
Nor scattered your treasure,
Nor raised an uproar in war,
Nor overrun your teeming people?
As though we had drained your beloved,
As though we had reaped your grain unripe,
As though we had plundered the domains
Of seven generations of ogre chieftains!
Why do you make trouble,
Descendant of warriors and heroes,
Why do you stand against us?
Is Talas such an easy land
That you might slaughter it,
Take it as spoil,
And dig out its roots before departing?
No migration of yours crossed the Seven Valleys,
You have no vengeance from seventy forefathers.
Do you possess the might, Sarybai,
To bring utter calamity?
Do you have the fury, Sarybai,
To fight until one of us is ended?
Did we tether mares in your valley,
Or settle upon your people’s land?
Did we massacre and despoil your village,
That you should glower so?
Did we slaughter your people,
That you should swagger and provoke strife?
If you are the hero Sarybai,
And I am the hero Külchoro,
A hero was the foe I sought;
What I asked of God,
What I prayed for, was you:
‘I knew of your enmity,
They advanced with noses running,
Their weapons numbering eighty-four,
Their onslaught blazing like fire.
When my father, the Ogre,
Saw Manas’s bearing,
He found no ridge to flee across,
No black earth to enter,
No grave in which to lie.
When eagle Bakai and hero Koshoy
Blocked the valley of Kerüüchö
Without letting anyone stir,
When Almambet wrought havoc,
And Chubak and hero Syrgak speared
The champions who shot in ranks
And plundered my countless wealth,
When my father, the Ogre,
Was slain by hero Manas,
They broke open my treasury and made a road through it,
And subdued my warriors,
Loading all my heaped-up riches
Upon my own elephants.
They tormented my very soul,
And plundered all my livestock.
They bewildered my people,
And bent my back many times.
They tasted much of my salt,
Then plundered and carried away
My needle-mouthed, camel-eyed,
Restless dark-eyed
Daughter, beautiful as this,
The strength around which I girded my belt,
And my people, diminished sixfold.
After long ruin I recovered,
I grew up while still in swaddling clothes.
I am a warrior and a hero;
I am Sarybai the champion!
I crush whoever challenges me,
I devour whoever meets me;
I am the black scourge itself!”
Skilled in the ways of war,
Külchoro said this to Sarybai,
And fierce fury seized him.
He ground apart
His broad, gate-like front teeth;
His eyes became burning embers,
His lashes blazing fire.
The warrior could not restrain
His surge, like a rushing river:
Sarybai was ready to fight.
Would a gray wolf hold back?
After Külchoro spoke thus,
The Ogre’s son answered,
Utterly dreadful words:
“If I do not slaughter your whole lineage,
If I do not do all the harm I know,
If I heed your words when you plead,
If I fail to avenge myself,
May I die unworthy of the name Sarybai;
May I sink into the depths unborn,
As though never born of the Ogre!
I have many words to tell,
And if you consider the horses wearied and lives tormented,
You will see how great my grievance is.
In Zhelpinish lived Jarmanas,
Whose wife was Karjygach;
She and Khan Manas were siblings.
They camped along the cliffs,
And, coming to Karjygach’s aid,
Gathered an army from the Kyrgyz.
The noble Bakai and hero Koshoy
Led an army such as this,
Loosing arrows in punishment,
Hiding by night and not marching by day.
They were warriors of many kinds,
Great Manas at the army’s head,
And Karjygach behind the host.
Plumed standards rose and banners thronged,
A dark and dreadful tumult arose,
Throwing the whole world into panic.
Beneath him, the great horse Kula
Made the earth thunder and mountains shift,
Tormenting every soul who heard,
As Sarybai sat astride it.
That infidel Sarybai
Charged like a wild boar.
The fierce courage of that swine
Was like a wind that shattered mountains and rocks.
His ferocity was like a quagmire;
All but the hero Külchoro
Seemed to collapse and fall.
Such was the warrior’s state,
The ruthless devourer Sarybai.
The infidel’s fury overflowed;
His roaring shook the valley.
Despairing of life and thinking themselves dead,
The teeming Argyn and Kyrgyz people,
Unable to collect their wits,
Fled amid the thunder.
Sarybai, son of the Ogre,
Seemed ready to reap destruction;
If the scoundrel had his way,
He would stuff the entire world
Into a single saddlebag.
His savage fury seemed all-consuming,
His strength ready to swallow lives.
Each hair upon his face
Was like the haft of a battle-ax.
The fierce courage of that swine
Was like flame burning across the uplands.
Such was Sarybai,
That blazing boar.
The earth split with a crash,
As he roared as though to devour them.
Like a crumbling mountain ledge,
Like a flood pouring down a slope,
Like a deep-dug grave,
The madman came upon them.
Firing his musket and drawing his bow,
Sarybai spared not his life;
He cursed again and showered arrows,
Never sated though he drank blood.
My resting place beneath the earth
Was there beside Zhelpinish.
“To unleash a terrible slaughter,
To avenge my father—
This alone was my desire.
My prowess is unlike any other,
My valor is beyond measure.
I shall make good the words I spoke;
How could I fail to avenge
The grievance famed among the people!
Ever since I became Sarybai,
I have defeated all who confronted me,
And swallowed all who charged me.
I have hewn down everyone I met,
And massacred and despoiled
Many champions and mighty giants who opposed me!
I speak to shatter your courage;
I shall slaughter many of you and take revenge!
I am the black eye of disaster,
Calamity itself.
No winged creature can escape me;
I am an impassable black precipice.
I am a dense forest of snares,
I swallow all who grapple with me.
I shall strike terror like a dragon,
And take my vengeance everywhere!
I am the very eye of calamity,
The black scourge itself.
I am a vast black valley
That cannot be exhausted even when shoveled away.”
So saying, Sarybai,
With fiery flame burning from his mouth,
Took a mountain-like mace in hand,
Struck Zhelmaian on the flank,
Broke through the narrows and opened a path,
And attacked Külchoro,
Standing there in wrath.
With his battle-ax he struck
The shrill-voiced brass spear.
Marking out the place of death,
The wonderfully vigilant hero
Külchoro stood waiting,
And against the infidel Ogre’s son
Thrust his spear upon reaching him.
As though he had punched a stone,
The noble man brought all his strength;
Its steel nature became evident:
The ornamented spear did not break,
But bent like a tent prop.
The wretched son of Almambet
Revealed himself a true hero,
Supremely vigilant and blessed with fortune,
His courage like a fortress of steel;
None who clashed with him could survive.
The ornamented spear had a steel core;
Thus he kept thrusting it.
If you ask about that ornamented spear,
It was designed and tempered for war.
Bölökbai, planning for battle,
Had fashioned it, poor man.
He hardened and twisted its shaft;
The master craftsman Bölökbai
Fitted and finished it beautifully.
He had iron drawn through its core,
And firmly increased its measure.
He edged it like a wolf’s tongue,
Lest by some chance in close combat
It slip from the hand,
And adorned it with lacquer.
Every bard sang of it,
And every discerning man listened.
If you ask about that ornamented spear,
When its charcoal was prepared,
A whole forest on the green plain was felled.
When its forge was fired,
A tribute bull of the Kyrgyz,
A blue young bull, was slaughtered.
He tempered its steel core,
Fashioning it expressly for battle,
And Külchoro drove it with tremendous force.
Raging and straining,
He again took in hand
The cast-iron head as large as a house,
And struck with that iron head.
Seizing the ornamented broad-mouthed arrow,
Sarybai shot a hundred shafts,
Summoning all his courage.
He made the age itself constrict,
As the madman stood thus.
